title: Perplexity Teammates: always-on AI agents that message your coworkers in Slack
content:
Perplexity’s AI agents keep working after you close the tab
Perplexity’s new Teammates can coordinate multiple agents, remember where previous sessions left off, and keep working without another prompt. The challenge is keeping everything in sync, especially when agents are working at the same time, sharing project state, and operating with different permissions.
Announced Wednesday, Teammates builds on infrastructure Perplexity has spent much of the year developing. The launch puts that earlier work to use in workflows where agents can delegate tasks and continue operating across sessions.
The challenge of keeping agents stateful
When Nate Kupp, Perplexity’s vice president of infrastructure, took The New Stack inside the company’s agent sandboxes, he described the difficulty of maintaining reliable systems at that scale.
“Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build,” Kupp said, pointing to the durability and uptime requirements of operating millions of sandboxes.
“Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build”
Teammates relies on Perplexity Computer’s existing infrastructure, which separates persistent project state from individual execution environments. That allows agents to continue working on the same project without depending on a single uninterrupted session.
Shared state lives in Git
In a technical breakdown of its shared workspaces, the company described how it uses Git-backed repositories to keep project state intact across sessions. Each Computer project has its own repository, while agents work in separate sandboxes and submit their changes back to the shared project.
That gets more complicated when agents are working on the same code at once since if one agent commits its changes first, another may have to reapply its work against the latest version.
Perplexity says fewer than 2% of submissions are rejected because they’re based on outdated repository state. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds.
Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds.
Memory is handled separately through Perplexity’s Brain system, which keeps what agents have learned in dedicated repositories. That lets background agents update shared knowledge without interfering with changes to the project’s files.
Pausing and forking agents
Perplexity built SPACE around Firecracker microVMs and Btrfs snapshots, making it possible to pause, resume, or fork agent sessions without losing their saved state.
With Teammates, developers can connect tools like Slack and GitHub and set up triggers that tell agents when to act. Perplexity hasn’t said much about what happens when that work gets stuck, particularly when one agent is waiting on another or acting on information that’s already out of date.
The open permission questions
Each teammate runs in its own isolated environment and browser session, with access managed through Computer’s existing permissions and credentials handled securely through encryption. Users can also monitor progress and take control when needed.
It’s unclear how it prevents agents from accessing resources beyond their permissions when tasks are handed off. For enterprises, that uncertainty could influence how much autonomy they’re willing to give agents without requiring human approval.
Teammates is initially available on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned.
Learning Path

report.summary: Perplexity launches Teammates, always-on AI agents that coordinate with each other, persist project state across sessions, and message coworkers in Slack without a new prompt.
report.background: Perplexity has spent most of 2025 building the plumbing for agents rather than just chat: isolated sandboxes, the Perplexity Computer execution layer, and a memory system called Brain. Teammates is the payoff — a product layer that turns that infrastructure into multi-agent workflows that survive beyond a single browser session. The move reflects a broader industry shift away from stateless chatbots toward 'stateful' agents that hold context, resume work, and hand tasks to each other. That is hard engineering: durable storage, conflict resolution and permission isolation all have to hold up at the scale of millions of sandboxes. Perplexity is also competing in an increasingly crowded orchestration space, where OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and a wave of open-source frameworks are all racing to own the layer where agents plan, delegate and remember.
key_points: Agents outlive the browser tab. Teammates can be paused, resumed or forked without losing state, built on Perplexity's SPACE system, which combines Firecracker microVMs with Btrfs snapshots. That means a task can keep running and pick up where it left off rather than restarting from scratch each session.

Project state lives in Git. Each Computer project has its own repository; agents work in separate sandboxes and commit changes back to the shared project. When two agents touch the same code, one may need to reapply its work — Perplexity says under 2% of submissions are rejected as stale, with median submission latency under 1.7 seconds.

Memory is kept separate from files. The Brain system stores what agents learn in dedicated repositories, so background agents can update shared knowledge without colliding with edits to the project itself — a clean split between 'what we know' and 'what we're building'.

Work is triggered by tools you already use. Developers connect Slack and GitHub and define triggers that tell agents when to act — including messaging coworkers — shifting agents from something you prompt to something that runs alongside your team.

Key questions remain unanswered. Perplexity has not detailed what happens when an agent stalls waiting on another, or how permissions are enforced when tasks are handed off between agents. That uncertainty matters for enterprises deciding how much autonomy to grant.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Teammates is a signal that the battleground has moved from model quality to orchestration and durability — who can keep many agents coherent, cheaply, for long periods. Git-backed shared state is a pragmatic, familiar answer to a genuinely hard distributed-systems problem, and rivals will likely converge on similar patterns. For developers, the appeal is real: long-running background work, resumable sessions, and Slack-native triggers reduce the glue code needed to build agentic workflows, though lock-in to Perplexity's sandbox stack is a risk. For regular users, the near-term change is subtle but significant — AI stops being a tab you visit and becomes a coworker that acts while you're away. The open permission model is the main brake on trust, especially in enterprises where an agent messaging colleagues unsupervised needs guardrails first.
report.tools: Worth watching: Perplexity Computer and Brain (the underlying sandbox and memory layers), Firecracker microVMs and Btrfs snapshots for anyone building pause/resume agent infrastructure. For open-source alternatives, look at Letta (formerly MemGPT) for stateful agent memory, Temporal for durable workflow orchestration, E2B or Modal for sandboxed code execution, and OpenHands or LangGraph for multi-agent coordination. Git-backed state patterns can be replicated today with plain repositories plus a job queue, which is a useful way to prototype before committing to a vendor.
